## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\begin{marginfigure}
\resizebox{0.92\linewidth}{!}{\mlphysicalstackfull{100}{20}{20}{20}{20}}
\end{marginfigure}
:::

_How do you translate ambiguous human language directives into mathematically grounded physical constraints that a real-time robot can safely execute?_

In disembodied machine learning systems, an autoregressive language model or vision-language foundation model operates entirely within discrete token spaces. If a model hallucinates an invalid syntax token, misclassifies an image region, or suffers a tail latency spike during KV-cache generation, the failure mode remains strictly confined to the digital domain: the runtime raises an exception, drops the output packet, or prompts the user for clarification. In physical AI, however, the downstream consumer of a high-level directive is not a text terminal or web interface; it is an array of pulse-width-modulated (PWM) inverter bridges commanding three-phase currents into motor windings. A motor inverter accepts electrical commutations, not linguistic tokens. Furthermore, because physical dynamics obey immutable conservation laws, software cannot undo kinetic energy once an actuator injects momentum into a moving link (@sec-boundary-causal-boundary). If an unconstrained neural network translates an open-ended command such as "pack the fragile mugs into the shipping box" directly into continuous motor commands, an empirical misclassification, depth triangulation error, or out-of-distribution visual hallucination commands physical impact, motor overcurrent trips, or destructive collisions with human coworkers and fragile workpieces.

The fundamental systems challenge of intent resolution is therefore not syntactic parsing or prompt engineering, but **semantic hallucination containment via capability sandboxing**. High-capacity deliberative models—spanning multi-billion-parameter Vision-Language-Action (VLA) backbones, diffusion score-matching policies, and multimodal transformers—run on unprivileged application processors under non-real-time operating systems subject to memory bus contention, page faults, and severe tail latency ($P_{99} \gg P_{50}$). These deliberative models must never hold open-ended authority over physical actuators. Instead, the architecture establishes a rigid privilege separation boundary: the unprivileged reasoning layer produces only typed, candidate *intent proposals*. The real-time safety monitor independently evaluates these proposals against geometric reachability manifolds, kinematic transit limits, and sensor evidence freshness before admitting them into execution. High-level semantic goals are transformed into bounded geometric affordance sets $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$, explicit spatial error envelopes, and effort ceilings on tool-center-point velocity and contact wrench. Finally, because the physical world evolves continuously while a deliberative model computes, intent resolution operates through time-bounded capability leases anchored to monotonic hardware clocks, ensuring that motion authority automatically revokes whenever physical evidence decays or upstream computation stalls. This chapter details the software contracts, geometric filters, and hardware lease mechanisms that convert unstructured multimodal directives into verifiable, mathematically grounded physical intent.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Ground natural-language directives into metric affordance frames, motion predicates, and verified geometric goal sets
- Emit the Intent Specification contract from parent belief records with explicit error envelopes, task tolerances, and effort ceilings
- Derive a target-evidence horizon from task tolerance and target drift, and distinguish it from the stopping deadline
- Decide when grounding ambiguity or a wrong-object premise requires refusal rather than admission
- Evaluate whether a proposed goal is reachable within its remaining evidence window
- Design lease expiry that revokes motion authority even when the issuing process cannot cancel it

:::

## Grounded Affordances {#sec-intent-grounded-affordances}

When the warehouse mobile manipulator is told to "pick the red mug" from the takeaway conveyor, the directive specifies an outcome but leaves path, force, and deadline unresolved. A motor inverter accepts electrical commands, not language. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [@brohan2023rt1; @brohan2023rt2] can propose actions or targets, but their update cadence depends on the model size and hardware accelerators, running at frequencies ($0.5\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$) orders of magnitude slower than local real-time control. If a target moves during neural inference, a stale proposal consumes physical clearance before execution even begins. The system therefore requires dated geometric evidence, bounded capability requests, and an independent permission path that can withdraw authority while the deliberative model is silent.

To an engineer trained on digital vision-language models, the directive "pick the mug" might sound like a solved classification task: a cross-attention map highlights the mug, and an autoregressive decoder outputs an action token. In embodied physics, however, grasping an object is not an isolated mathematical point; it is an action-relative relation governed by geometric **affordances**\index{Affordances!grasp envelopes} [@gibson1979ecological]. Each functional feature on an object establishes an **affordance coordinate frame** $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ rigidly attached to the object's body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{obj}}$. For the red mug, the rim affordance frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{rim}}$ requires low gripping force to avoid crushing fragile ceramic or spilling liquid; the cylindrical body frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{body}}$ requires wide parallel finger span and high normal force to prevent slipping; the handle affordance frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{handle}}$ requires a six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) approach vector that aligns the gripper fingers with the ear of the mug while respecting joint travel and torque limits.

Intent grounding bridges this chasm by translating high-level semantic directives into continuous **motion predicates**\index{Motion predicates!definition} evaluated over these metric coordinate frames:

1. *Pre-contact approach predicate:* $P_{\text{approach}}(\mathbf{x}) \iff \|\mathbf{p}_{\text{TCP}} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{pre}}\| \le r_{\text{tol}} \land \arccos(\hat{\mathbf{z}}_{\text{TCP}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}) \le \theta_{\text{tol}}$, requiring the end effector tool center point (TCP, the coordinate origin at the robot's gripper tip—distinct from the network Transmission Control Protocol) frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{TCP}}$ to align with the affordance approach axis $\hat{\mathbf{a}}_{\text{approach}}$ within spatial tolerance $r_{\text{tol}}$ and angular tolerance $\theta_{\text{tol}}$.
2. *Guarded contact predicate:* $P_{\text{contact}}(\mathbf{w}) \iff f_{\min} \le \|\mathbf{f}_{\text{contact}}\| \le f_{\max}$, ensuring that contact forces remain sufficient for friction grip while strictly bounded below structural crush limits.
3. *Spatial clearance predicate:* $P_{\text{clear}}(\mathbf{x}, \mathcal{M}) \iff \min_{\mathbf{o} \in \mathcal{M}} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{o}\| \ge d_{\text{margin}}$, verifying collision-free swept volume against the spatial memory state $\mathcal{M}$ (@sec-memory).

Together, these predicates bound the allowable terminal configurations into a formal **geometric goal set** $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$\index{SE(3)!target goal set}:
$$\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} = \left\{ \mathbf{T} = (\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{p}) \in SE(3) \;\middle|\; \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{target}}\|_{\mathbf{E}} \le 1, \; \angle(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) \le \theta_{\text{tol}} \right\}$$ {#eq-intent-goal-set-se3}
where $\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}_{\text{target}}\|_{\mathbf{E}} = \sqrt{\sum_{i \in \{x,y,z\}} \left(\frac{p_i - p_{\text{target},i}}{r_i}\right)^2}$ denotes spatial containment within the task tolerance ellipsoid with principal semi-axes $\mathbf{r} = (r_x, r_y, r_z)$, and $\angle(\mathbf{R}, \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) = \arccos\left(\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{R}_{\text{target}}) - 1}{2}\right)$ bounds geodesic orientation divergence on $SO(3)$ (equivalent to $2 \arccos(|\mathbf{q} \cdot \mathbf{q}_{\text{target}}|)$ when orientations are represented as unit quaternions). If a controller attempts to command an end-effector pose outside $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}$, the physical task fails: position error exceeding $r_i$ causes the gripper fingers to strike the mug rim or close on empty air, while angular tilt beyond $\theta_{\text{tol}}$ jams the fingers against the handle opening, tripping joint torque monitors or shattering the workpiece.

Before any candidate affordance is packaged into an intent proposal, the system executes **affordance validation and scoring**\index{Affordances!validation}\index{Affordances!scoring}. When open-vocabulary foundation models predict multiple candidate grasp frames on an object, an affordance scoring function ranks candidate frames by evaluating kinematic manipulability $\mu(\mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\det(\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})\mathbf{J}^\top(\mathbf{q}))}$ (penalizing singular joint configurations near workspace boundaries), geometric approach clearance against spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$, and gripper jaw opening margins. The intent engine confirms whether the candidate frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ is kinematically reachable within the manipulator's workspace manifold $\mathcal{W}$, whether the gripper jaw aperture clears the object width, and whether a collision-free approach cone exists. If validation fails or candidate referents remain unresolved, the system must not execute an ungrounded guess; it triggers an explicit **intent grounding refusal**\index{Intent grounding refusal!definition} (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The belief record a lease consumes (evidence epoch, initial error, growth law) is specified in @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema.
:::

Memory can supply a spatial belief with an expiry (@sec-memory-belief-through-occlusion); it cannot decide what action that belief authorizes. **Intent**\index{Intent} closes that gap by connecting high-level task semantics to a bounded physical goal. It specifies an admissible, time-bounded target before the trajectory planner of @sec-planning constructs a continuous motion profile to reach it.

Connecting words to physical targets is the robotics form of what Harnad termed the **symbol grounding problem**\index{Symbol grounding problem} [@harnad1990symbol]: purely symbolic or linguistic tokens within a computational system have no intrinsic physical meaning unless causally grounded in non-symbolic, sensorimotor interactions with the physical environment.[^fn-intent-symbol-grounding] In disembodied language models, an ungrounded or hallucinated token incurs only conversational error; in physical AI, commanding an ungrounded token translates semantic hallucination directly into physical damage.[^fn-intent-hallucination-containment] Modern physical AI systems must therefore sandbox open-vocabulary instructions into continuous, dynamic, and uncertain metric spaces, containing semantic uncertainty before motion authority is granted.[^fn-intent-affordance-space]

[^fn-intent-symbol-grounding]: **Symbol Grounding Problem**\index{Symbol Grounding Problem}: Stevan Harnad's 1990 formulation argues that syntactic manipulation alone does not give symbols intrinsic meaning. In physical AI, grounding binds a proposed label to dated sensor evidence, calibrated metric frames, and task-specific physical checks. Without that binding, a planner may optimize toward the wrong physical target.

[^fn-intent-hallucination-containment]: **Semantic hallucination containment**\index{Safety!hallucination containment}\index{Grounding!semantic containment}: Unlike disembodied text generation where hallucinations degrade conversational coherence, robotic hallucinations command physical momentum. Containment requires packaging high-level outputs into typed proposal contracts with verifiable metric bounds before execution.

[^fn-intent-affordance-space]: **Affordance space parameterization**\index{Affordances!spatial parameterization}: In robot learning, affordances are parameterized as continuous spatial probability fields or reachability manifolds over the Lie group $SE(3)$. Parameterizing reachability as an explicit manifold enables low-level controllers to evaluate physical feasibility before invoking computationally intensive trajectory optimizers.

::: {#dfn-intent-grounding-refusal .callout-definition title="Intent grounding refusal"}

***Intent grounding refusal***\index{Intent grounding refusal!definition}\index{Refusal!grounding ambiguity} is the admission rule whereby an embodied system explicitly rejects semantically ambiguous natural-language directives, returning a typed failure status (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`) rather than executing ungrounded maximum-likelihood guesses across physical clearance margins.

1.  **Significance**: Rejects a proposal when a task-specific ambiguity test (@sec-intent-failure-modes) fails, before that proposal reaches trajectory generation.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a trajectory planning failure that cannot find a collision-free path to a valid goal, grounding refusal rejects the goal itself as physically ungrounded or ambiguous before the planner is invoked.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Forcing an argmax token decode or nearest-neighbor guess when candidate referents remain unresolved, driving the physical plant toward an arbitrary or hazardous target.

:::

Whatever the model proposes must also remain bounded in time. @Fig-intent-frequency-gap gives a schedule in which a slow deliberative model, local tracker, permission loop, and drive run at different rates. A common misconception among machine learning practitioners is that compiling or distilling a vision-language-action policy (via INT4 quantization, speculative decoding, or TensorRT) to run at $50\text{ Hz}$ eliminates the need for modular intent leases. However, average throughput on an edge operating system does not guarantee deterministic real-time deadlines: Linux scheduling jitter, memory bus contention, and sensor dropouts create severe tail latency ($P_{99} \gg P_{50}$). More fundamentally, an unconstrained statistical neural network lacks formal mathematical bounds against hallucinating full-scale reverse torque steps or out-of-bounds reach requests. Accelerating neural throughput changes execution speed, not epistemic trust; tail jitter, sensor dropouts, and non-Lipschitz neural hallucinations still require an independent deterministic safety gate armed with monotonic countdown leases. A conveyor target whose evidence expires within tens of milliseconds cannot be renewed by a model updating every few hundred milliseconds, so it requires a separate validated local observation path or a task pause. The figure's rates are illustrative, and @sec-intent-goals-expire sets the machine's own intent cadence against the conveyor horizon.

↩ The proposal boundary and the permission path are defined in @sec-boundary-machine-model.
:::

Grounding an open-ended directive therefore ends in a dated **intent proposal**, which the application processor sends across the proposal boundary. It requests bounds in space, time, and effort, and the independent permission path tests each against configured limits, current state, and stopping clearance before motion begins.

## The Intent Handoff and Bounded Authority {#sec-intent-handoff}

When the arm reaches for the red mug, the Brain sends neither joint trajectories nor winding voltages across the proposal boundary. In modern physical AI architectures, this boundary represents a fundamental capability-based security interface: the unprivileged application processor (hosting the neural network weights under Linux) possesses zero hardware capabilities to toggle inverter gate drives, assert PWM commutations, or modify motor current setpoints directly. Granting an uncertified neural model direct write access to actuator registers would mean that any operating system deadlock, out-of-memory kernel panic, or inference tail latency spike would leave moving physical mass unguided. Instead, the deliberative layer communicates across the proposal boundary purely through typed, candidate capability requests.

The real-time permission path evaluates every field of this request before admitting any portion of it into execution. The checks span four mandatory invariants: target spatial tolerance, sensor evidence freshness, requested dynamic effort, and a pre-certified deterministic fallback. Each invariant exists because a delayed or erroneous proposal can fail in a distinct physical mode: an unmodeled target coordinate breaches collision margins, a stale timestamp consumes clearance, an uncapped force shatters a workpiece, and an unverified fallback leaves the robot without a feasible stopping trajectory if the host crashes. In the machine stack's contract lineage, this handoff is formalized as the **Intent Specification** (Contract 9). Emitted downstream to the trajectory planner (@sec-planning) as an admitted **Intent Lease** record, it provides certified geometric goal sets, affordance frame bindings, and verified motion predicates that constrain continuous spline generation. @Sec-intent-lease details the schema and lineage of this record.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/spa_locator_p.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="S·P·A locator triad highlighting the Plan node."}
*The Plan node: generating bounded intent leases that constrain autonomous action within verifiable safety limits.*
:::

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ The running machine's intent horizons, the arm's transit lower bound, the   │
# │ mug intent lapse and its arm stop onset, the latch contact at brake command,│
# │ and the Class 3 plant.                                                      │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import (
    fmt_latency,
    fmt_length,
    fmt_velocity,
    fmt_acceleration,
    fmt_frequency,
    fmt_force,
    fmt_force_rate,
    fmt_heat_capacity,
    fmt_power,
    fmt_temperature,
    fmt_temperature_rate,
    fmt_sci_qty,
    check,
)
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import (
    calc_target_evidence_horizon,
    calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile,
    calc_contact_force,
)

# ┌── 1. LOAD: the running machine, plus chapter-local scenario inputs ─────────
RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator  # category: illustrative (running machine)
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle  # category: illustrative (aisle scene; lease chosen)

delta_t_stall_intent = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (stalled proposer holds the mug target)
delta_t_stall_arm = 200.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (unbraked contact interval)
v_drift_slow = 20.0 * millimeter / second  # category: illustrative (slow-drift case in the figure)
t_intent_tail = 650.0 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (high-tail intent inference, as in the figure)
d_target_offset = 300.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (scenario assumption: gripper-to-handle distance at proposal)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: evidence horizons, mug intent lapse, latch contact ───────────
# Mug on the conveyor: untracked and tracked target-evidence horizons. Both
# horizons charge the 3 mm initial error against the 15 mm tolerance.
grasp_error_budget = (AISLE.grasp_tolerance - AISLE.grasp_initial_error).to(millimeter)
tau_ev_untracked = calc_target_evidence_horizon(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, AISLE.grasp_initial_error, AISLE.v_conveyor).to(millisecond)
tau_ev_tracked = ((2 * grasp_error_budget / AISLE.a_conveyor_slip) ** 0.5).to(millisecond)
t_intent_period = (1.0 / RM.intent_rate).to(millisecond)
err_at_intent_period = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + AISLE.v_conveyor * t_intent_period).to(millimeter)
err_excess_at_period = (err_at_intent_period - AISLE.grasp_tolerance).to(millimeter)
t_tail_overrun = (t_intent_tail - tau_ev_untracked).to(millisecond)
tau_ev_slow_drift = calc_target_evidence_horizon(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, AISLE.grasp_initial_error, v_drift_slow).to(millisecond)

# Dynamic reachability: the TCP speed ceiling bounds the reach inside the tracked
# horizon, and a proposal farther away fails the transit lower bound.
d_reach_tracked = (RM.tcp_speed_limit * tau_ev_tracked).to(millimeter)
d_reach_untracked = (RM.tcp_speed_limit * tau_ev_untracked).to(millimeter)
t_transit_floor = (d_target_offset / RM.tcp_speed_limit).to(millisecond)

# Mug intent lapse: a stalled proposer holds the target; untracked drift at the
# conveyor speed, tracked drift from residual slip only; arm stop onset after
# intent expiry is one permission tick, one bus cycle, and the brake onset.
err_stalled_untracked = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + AISLE.v_conveyor * delta_t_stall_intent).to(millimeter)
err_stalled_tracked = (AISLE.grasp_initial_error + 0.5 * AISLE.a_conveyor_slip * delta_t_stall_intent**2).to(millimeter)
t_arm_onset_after_expiry = (AISLE.t_tick + AISLE.t_bus + AISLE.t_brake_onset).to(millisecond)

# Latch contact: force at brake command, then the arm stop that keeps it under the limit.
latch_profile = calc_latch_contact_stopping_profile(scenario=AISLE)
df_dt = latch_profile["df_dt"]
f_at_brake_onset = latch_profile["f_at_brake_onset"]
x_remaining = latch_profile["x_remaining"]
a_arm_needed = latch_profile["a_arm_needed"]
t_arm_stop = latch_profile["t_arm_stop"]
delta_x_unbounded = (AISLE.v_latch_approach * delta_t_stall_arm).to(millimeter)
f_unbounded = calc_contact_force(AISLE.k_latch, delta_x_unbounded)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: canon values quoted in the prose ──────────────────────────────
check(abs(tau_ev_untracked.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, "Untracked mug horizon is 60 ms")
check(abs(tau_ev_tracked.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, "Tracked mug horizon is 219 ms")
check(abs(grasp_error_budget.magnitude - 12.0) < 1e-6, "Mug error budget is 12 mm")
check(abs(err_stalled_untracked.magnitude - 43.0) < 1e-6, "Stalled untracked target sits 43 mm off")
check(abs(err_stalled_tracked.magnitude - 13.0) < 1e-6, "Stalled tracked target sits 13 mm off")
check(abs(t_arm_onset_after_expiry.magnitude - 22.0) < 1e-6, "Arm stop onset within 22 ms of intent expiry")
check(abs(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, "TCP speed ceiling is 1.0 m/s")
check(abs(t_intent_period.magnitude - 200.0) < 1e-6, "5 Hz intent period is 200 ms")
check(abs(err_at_intent_period.magnitude - 43.0) < 1e-6, "Error at the intent period")
check(abs(tau_ev_slow_drift.magnitude - 600.0) < 1e-6, "Slow-drift horizon in the figure")
check(abs(t_tail_overrun.magnitude - 590.0) < 1e-6, "Tail overrun past the untracked horizon is 590 ms")
check(abs(d_reach_tracked.magnitude - 219.09) < 5e-3, "TCP reach inside the tracked horizon is 219 mm")
check(abs(d_reach_untracked.magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-6, "TCP reach inside the untracked horizon is 60 mm")
check(abs(t_transit_floor.magnitude - 300.0) < 1e-6, "Transit floor for the offset proposal is 300 ms")
check(t_transit_floor > tau_ev_tracked, "Offset proposal fails the transit lower bound")
check(abs(AISLE.t_lease.to(millisecond).magnitude - 60.0) < 1e-9, "Chunk lease is 60 ms")
check(abs(f_at_brake_onset.to(newton).magnitude - 39.0) < 1e-9, "Force at brake command")
check(abs(x_remaining.magnitude - 0.1525) < 5e-5, "Latch compression left is 0.15 mm")
check(abs(a_arm_needed.magnitude - 2.95) < 5e-3, "Arm stop premise is about 3 m/s^2 (2.95)")
check(abs(t_arm_stop.magnitude - 10.0) < 0.5, "Arm stop takes about 10 ms")
check(abs(f_unbounded.to(newton).magnitude - 2400.0) < 1.0, "Unbraked contact model")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ──────────────────────────────────────────────
class IntentLeaseArchetypes:
    # Mug on the conveyor
    v_conveyor_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_conveyor, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    r_tol_str = fmt_length(AISLE.grasp_tolerance, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    e0_str = fmt_length(AISLE.grasp_initial_error, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    tau_untracked_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_untracked, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    tau_tracked_str = fmt_latency(round(tau_ev_tracked.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    a_slip_str = fmt_acceleration(AISLE.a_conveyor_slip, unit=meter / second**2, precision=2)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(RM.intent_rate, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_intent_period_str = fmt_latency(t_intent_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_infer_str = fmt_latency(RM.intent_inference_latency, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    err_at_period_str = fmt_length(err_at_intent_period, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    err_excess_str = fmt_length(err_excess_at_period, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    v_drift_slow_str = fmt_velocity(v_drift_slow, unit=millimeter / second, precision=0)
    tau_slow_drift_str = fmt_latency(tau_ev_slow_drift, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_intent_tail_str = fmt_latency(t_intent_tail, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tail_overrun_str = fmt_latency(round(t_tail_overrun.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    # Dynamic reachability on the arm
    d_reach_tracked_str = fmt_length(round(d_reach_tracked.magnitude) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_reach_untracked_str = fmt_length(d_reach_untracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_target_str = fmt_length(d_target_offset, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_transit_floor_str = fmt_latency(t_transit_floor, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    # Mug intent lapse and the admitted mug lease
    err_budget_str = fmt_length(grasp_error_budget, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_stall_intent_str = fmt_latency(delta_t_stall_intent, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    err_stalled_untracked_str = fmt_length(err_stalled_untracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    err_stalled_tracked_str = fmt_length(err_stalled_tracked, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    t_arm_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_arm_onset_after_expiry, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_tcp_str = fmt_velocity(RM.tcp_speed_limit.to(meter / second))
    # Latch contact
    k_latch_str = fmt_sci_qty(AISLE.k_latch, newton / meter, precision=1)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(AISLE.v_latch_approach, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_tripwire, precision=0)
    t_contact_str = fmt_latency(AISLE.t_contact_response, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    df_dt_nms_str = fmt_force_rate(df_dt, unit=newton / millisecond, precision=0)
    f_at_brake_onset_n_str = fmt_force(f_at_brake_onset, precision=0)
    f_lim_str = fmt_force(AISLE.f_latch_limit, precision=0)
    x_remaining_str = fmt_length(round(x_remaining.magnitude, 2) * millimeter, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    a_arm_str = fmt_acceleration(round(a_arm_needed.magnitude) * meter / second**2, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    t_arm_stop_str = fmt_latency(round(t_arm_stop.magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_stall_arm_str = fmt_latency(delta_t_stall_arm, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    delta_x_unbounded_mm_str = fmt_length(delta_x_unbounded, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    f_unbounded_n_str = fmt_force(f_unbounded, precision=0, commas=True)
    # Permission loop
    f_permission_str = fmt_frequency(RM.permission_rate, unit=ureg.kHz, precision=0)
```

In physical manipulation, specifying an isolated target coordinate is an incomplete and hazardous abstraction. In ecological psychology, an affordance is an action-relative relation among geometry, robot reach, and contact limits [@gibson1979ecological]. In ML systems, an unconstrained neural prediction $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ exhibits continuous stochastic variance across inference cycles. Forcing a low-level controller to converge toward an exact mathematical point causes infinite settling times, asymptotic hunting, and high-frequency torque chatter as the motor drive expends current attempting to eliminate microscopic sensor noise. The intent proposal therefore requests a target pose in $SE(3)$, the Lie group of three-dimensional positions and orientations, paired with an explicit **task tolerance region**\index{Tolerance region!3D spatial}\index{Intent record!spatial tolerance region} within which the manipulation objective is formally satisfied. This task tolerance differs fundamentally from the estimator's covariance: covariance represents epistemic uncertainty about the target's true state, whereas task tolerance defines the physical error volume permissible before the task fails. For the machine's mug grasp, the approved task profile allows `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` of translational error. A trajectory controller can then terminate cleanly within that tolerance volume rather than integrating tracking errors indefinitely; the permission path verifies that the estimated target uncertainty envelope fits strictly inside this tolerance boundary.

Spatial validity in the physical world is transient and non-stationary. A physical goal must therefore carry an explicit evidence epoch and a finite requested expiry\index{Intent record!temporal lease}, rather than relying on an asynchronous cancellation message[^fn-anti-async-abort] dispatched from the deliberative reasoning layer. In distributed software architectures, processes cancel pending RPCs or dispatch `SIGTERM` signals when work becomes obsolete. In physical systems, however, relying on an unprivileged host to send an asynchronous abort packet is a dangerous antipattern: the exact failure that necessitates an emergency abort—such as an operating system kernel lockup, memory allocation stall, or inference timeout—is the very failure that prevents the cancellation packet from ever being dispatched. A deliberative model that produces a new proposal only once per planning cycle cannot, even in the absence of system jitter, renew a target whose physical evidence expires in a shorter duration. An independent permission controller evaluates the admitted deadline on each real-time control tick and drops tracking authority autonomously when the evidence or lease lapses. When tracking lapses, the controller selects a pre-configured, validated hold or stop profile matched to the measured physical state and remaining clearance.[^fn-std-iso-watchdog] The local hardware countdown timer eliminates runtime dependence on host abort messages, while physical stopping distance remains an immutable kinetic constraint.

[^fn-std-iso-watchdog]: **Hardware watchdog safety monitors**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}\index{Safety standards!ISO 13849}: A safety design can use an independently clocked watchdog to detect missed renewals and initiate a validated response without the host. Safe Torque Off removes drive torque; it does not by itself hold a suspended load or stop moving mass within a specified clearance.

[^fn-anti-async-abort]: **Asynchronous Safety Event Dispatch**\index{Antipatterns!asynchronous safety cancellation}: Relying on asynchronous cancellation messages or network event dispatch to abort motion introduces non-deterministic queue serialization delays, and every millisecond of that delay is unbraked travel at the base's drive limit. A local countdown can revoke tracking authority on missed renewal.

A target bounded in space and time remains dangerous if the controller is granted unlimited physical effort. The intent proposal therefore requests explicit effort ceilings\index{Intent record!force limits} on tool-center-point velocity, acceleration, and contact wrench. If a vision backbone localizes a surface with small stereo disparity error, placing a goal coordinate two millimeters inside a rigid workpiece, a stiff proportional-integral-derivative (PID) position controller will saturate motor currents attempting to eliminate the position error, damaging the gearbox or crushing the object. For the arm's guarded approach to the spring-latched cage door, the proposal requests the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire as its contact-force ceiling, well below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` structural latch limit, and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` approach speed as its velocity cap. The permission path compares each request against independently configured actuator torque-speed limits and task ceilings, admitting only a safe, feasible subset. The low-level **impedance controller**\index{Impedance controller}[^fn-ctrl-impedance-intent] enforces these admitted limits by dynamically modulating mechanical compliance.

[^fn-ctrl-impedance-intent]: **Mechanical impedance regulation**\index{Control systems!impedance control}: Impedance control regulates the relation between contact force and motion through effective mass, damping, and stiffness. It can reduce loads within a validated contact regime; the first impact and peak force still depend on approach speed, passive compliance, sensing, and actuator response.

Omitting any of these three bounds leaves a physical machine exposed during communication dropouts or perception stalls. Kinetic stopping distance grows linearly with the delay before braking onset and quadratically with physical velocity (@eq-body-stopping-distance). On a mobile base, whose stopping budget is a spatial clearance, a stalled proposer lengthens the delay term by the entire duration its last proposal retains execution authority. That duration is the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences, and it directly inflates the unbraked latency term $\tau_{\text{delay}}$. Physical clearance holds if and only if an independently verified obstacle boundary lies beyond this cumulative stopping distance, accounting for sensor latencies and model uncertainty margins.

The intent lease is a distinct architectural construct. It bounds how long a high-level semantic target remains physically justified, and its expiration revokes tracking authority over that target immediately, transitioning the plant to a safe terminal state without inflating the mobile base's stopping budget.

::: {#nbk-intent-lease-duration-collision-exposure-tradeoff-across .callout-notebook title="Lapsed authority and physical response"}

The two quantitative models below evaluate the physical consequences of stalled computation across distinct manipulation regimes. A stopping calculation requires the total delay to brake onset and the deceleration available from the *current* measured physical state:

1. **The mug intent lapse:** The manipulator reaches for the red mug under an intent proposal admitted without local tracking. At conveyor speed `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_conveyor_str`, the conveyor consumes the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_budget_str` error budget between the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str` initial localization error and the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance in `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`. Consequently, the target's sensor evidence expires at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`, as formalized in the mug-handle belief record of @sec-memory-spatial-state-schema. Suppose the application processor stalls during neural inference. A target held for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` by the frozen proposer would sit `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_untracked_str` away from the physical mug, guaranteeing that the gripper fingers close on empty air or strike the rim. The intent lease does not wait for a host recovery packet: at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_untracked_str`, the lease expires, tracking authority terminates, and the arm initiates a controlled stop with onset within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_onset_str` (spanning one permission loop tick, one fieldbus cycle, and actuator brake onset). The chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences serves as the ultimate hardware backstop if software expiry fails. By contrast, under an active local tracker running at $50\text{ Hz}$, the same `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_intent_str` inference stall leaves the target only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.err_stalled_tracked_str` off—safely inside the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` tolerance—because the tracked evidence horizon derived in @sec-intent-goals-expire extends to `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.tau_tracked_str`. Local high-rate tracking is what renders a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_intent_str` deliberative intent refresh rate viable.
2. **The arm at the cage door:** In mechanical contact with stiff physical environments, contact force does not rise gradually; for contact stiffness $k$, force escalates at the rate $\frac{df}{dt} = k \cdot v_{\text{approach}}$. At the guarded approach speed of `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.v_latch_str` against the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.k_latch_str` strike plate of the cage door, modeled contact force rises at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.df_dt_nms_str` ($20\text{ N/ms}$). A `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_trip_str` tripwire threshold combined with a `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_contact_str` contact-loop response yields `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_at_brake_onset_n_str` **at the exact instant the brake command begins**; force continues to rise rapidly while actuator inertia decelerates. Staying strictly below the `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_lim_str` latch yield limit leaves only `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.x_remaining_str` of allowable mechanical compression, requiring the arm to decelerate at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.a_arm_str` and come to rest within `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_arm_stop_str`. Whether the manipulator can sustain that peak deceleration depends on actuator torque limits and link inertia. If unbraked motion continues for `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.t_stall_arm_str` due to a delayed abort command, the gripper advances `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.delta_x_unbounded_mm_str` past initial contact, generating `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.f_unbounded_n_str` in the linear-spring contact model—vastly exceeding structural yield limits and destroying the mechanism.
:::

These two scenarios clarify the strict division of authority in physical AI. High-level deliberative reasoning models propose a candidate target, temporal execution window, and effort ceilings. The independent real-time permission path evaluates which limits are admissible given current physical state, configured plant envelopes, and certified stopping trajectories. Local low-level control tracks only an admitted proposal, revoking authority immediately upon evidence expiration or invariant breach. This establishes a strict **privilege separation boundary**\index{Privilege separation!intent boundary}[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent] between unprivileged neural proposers and privileged real-time supervisors, generalizing the behavioral priority separation of early reactive systems [@brooks1986robust].

[^fn-ai-subsumption-intent]: **Privilege separation in behavioral layers**\index{Architecture!subsumption}\index{Control!subsumption}: Rodney Brooks's subsumption architecture established priority-arbitrated behavioral layers on sensory feedback. In physical AI systems, this architecture manifests as an unprivileged deliberative layer proposing targets to a privileged real-time supervisor that validates invariants and enforces safe fallbacks.

Grounding an intent proposal into these three bounds requires a formal transformation from ambiguous sensory inputs into structured, verifiable proposals. When a system processes a high-level directive or a sequence of visual tokens, the initial proposal is rarely a single, unambiguous set of coordinates. It begins as an uncertain geometric hypothesis that must carry its own spatial ambiguity and its own temporal limits before it can be admitted to the execution pipeline.

## Semantic Request Translation to Geometric Proposals {#sec-intent-request-to-proposal}

A natural language instruction becomes dangerous when an unverified semantic hypothesis commands motion. When an operator or high-level supervisor asks for the red mug, an onboard vision-language foundation model parses the character stream, projects image features into a shared embedding space, and selects a candidate visual bounding region. From those pixels, the network extracts an estimated pose in $SE(3)$ and writes coordinate values into a memory buffer. At the proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), an ungrounded string of tokens becomes a requested destination; if admitted, it reaches the causal boundary as mass, velocity, and current.[^fn-math-semantic-metric]

If the visual backbone associates the language token with an adjacent fixture or an unlabeled calibration target, the resulting coordinate vector $\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3$ enters the trajectory pipeline as an authoritative physical goal. Because a low-level motor drive measures only encoder pulses, winding temperatures, and phase currents, it cannot evaluate whether the coordinate it tracks corresponds to the intended mug or to an empty stretch of belt.[^fn-math-vlm-lipschitz] Furthermore, extrinsic transform errors ($\Delta \mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}$) arising from wrist mounting compliance, mechanical payloads, thermal expansion, or link elasticity propagate directly into metric goal bias. High semantic confidence from a vision backbone masks underlying geometric calibration drift, reinforcing why the proposal must carry conservative base-frame error bounds rather than raw point coordinates. The grounding process must produce an explicit geometric proposal that includes spatial uncertainty, selection evidence, and temporal expiration before any motion planner accepts it.

[^fn-math-semantic-metric]: **Semantic-to-metric transformation**\index{Kinematics!semantic-to-metric}\index{Grounding!metric mapping}: Projecting discrete linguistic embeddings into continuous $SE(3)$ coordinates requires an unbroken coordinate calibration chain from image pixels to actuator base frames. Unmodeled camera mounting compliance or lens distortion maps semantic attention peaks into systematic metric offsets. If the transformation chain lacks rigid extrinsic calibration, high semantic confidence produces large physical tracking errors at the end effector.

[^fn-math-vlm-lipschitz]: **Learned-output sensitivity**\index{Neural network!Lipschitz continuity}\index{Safety!Lipschitz bounds}: A learned pose estimate can change substantially when the image or scene changes, and an empirical confidence score does not bound that change. The permission path limits the admitted target and motion using independently checked geometry, state, and actuator constraints.

### The four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline {#sec-intent-four-stage-pipeline}

To systematize the wide variety of modern foundation-model-driven robotics frameworks—ranging from task-ranking networks [@ahn2022saycan] and code synthesizers [@huang2023voxposer; @liang2023code] to open-vocabulary grasp generators [@liu2024okrobot] and end-to-end vision-language-action policies [@brohan2023rt1; @kim2024openvla]—we formulate the canonical **four-stage open-vocabulary grounding pipeline**:

1. **Stage 1: Multimodal Perception & Visual Feature Encoding**: High-bandwidth visual streams (RGB-D frames from static cameras or eye-in-hand sensors) are ingested alongside proprioceptive joint states. Executing at batch size one ($B=1$) on edge NPUs or GPUs, a deep vision backbone (such as a Vision Transformer with $14\times14$ patch tokenization, CLIP visual encoder, or convolutional feature pyramid) extracts dense spatial feature embeddings that encode both fine geometry and visual semantics.
2. **Stage 2: 2D Semantic Referent Selection & Open-Vocabulary Prompt Grounding**: Given an unconstrained natural language prompt (e.g., "pick the red ceramic mug"), cross-attention mechanisms align linguistic tokens with visual patch embeddings. Modern open-vocabulary grounding models—such as Grounding DINO [@liu2023grounding], OWL-ViT, or PaliGemma—compute attention heatmaps and predict candidate 2D bounding boxes, instance segmentation masks, or normalized spatial location tokens identifying physical referents in image pixel space $(u, v)$.
3. **Stage 3: Metric 3D Lifting & Workspace Unprojection**: Using calibrated camera intrinsic parameters $\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ and synchronized optical depth returns $z = d(u, v)$, the selected 2D pixel coordinates are unprojected into metric camera coordinates: $\mathbf{x}_{\text{cam}} = z \mathbf{K}^{-1} [u, v, 1]^\top$. Applying the rigid extrinsic transform from the camera frame to the robot base frame, $\mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}} \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$, transforms the point into base-frame workspace coordinates: $\mathbf{x}_{\text{base}} = \mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}} \mathbf{x}_{\text{cam}}$. Any optical depth distortion, specular dropouts, or extrinsic calibration drift ($\Delta \mathbf{T}_{\text{base} \leftarrow \text{cam}}$ caused by link compliance or thermal deflection) propagates directly into spatial displacement at this stage.
4. **Stage 4: Affordance Parameterization & Candidate Goal Generation**: The lifted metric geometry is converted into actionable manipulation hypotheses. Depending on the architecture, this output may take the form of 6-DoF grasp envelopes with approach cones, continuous 3D attraction/repulsion cost fields [@huang2023voxposer], parameterized motion primitives [@liang2023code], or 256-bin action token distributions [@brohan2023rt1]. Crucially, Stage 4 scores candidate affordance frames $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ by evaluating kinematic manipulability $\mu(\mathbf{q}) = \sqrt{\det(\mathbf{J}\mathbf{J}^\top)}$ and collision margins against spatial memory $\mathcal{M}$. It then parameterizes candidate geometric goal sets $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}} \subset SE(3)$ around validated affordance frames and specifies the target motion predicates ($P_{\text{approach}}, P_{\text{contact}}, P_{\text{clear}}$) required for task completion.

Across the physical silicon boundary between the non-real-time Linux Application Processor (AP) and the hard real-time Safety MCU, Stage 4 serializes these hypotheses into a fixed-size, statically verified proposal structure (@tbl-10-intent-proposal-fields).

\Needspace{22\baselineskip}

| Field                  | Representation       | Physical semantics                                                                              | Invariant and admission check                                                         |
|:-----------------------|:---------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `evidence_epoch_ns`    | `uint64_t` (ns)      | Sensor capture timestamp $t_0$ from parent belief record                                        | Must match retained belief epoch; reject if stale or unrecorded                       |
| `affordance_frame_id`  | `uint32_t` (enum)    | Target coordinate frame $\mathcal{F}_{\text{affordance}}$ (e.g., $\mathcal{F}_{\text{handle}}$) | Must resolve to an approved kinematic frame on the target object                      |
| `predicate_mask`       | `uint32_t` (bitmask) | Requested motion predicates ($P_{\text{approach}}, P_{\text{contact}}, P_{\text{clear}}$)       | Verified against task requirements before planner invocation                          |
| `target_pose_se3`      | `double[7]`          | Proposed pose $[x, y, z, q_x, q_y, q_z, q_w]$ in robot base frame                               | Finite values; unit quaternion ($\lVert \mathbf{q} \rVert = 1$); within $\mathcal{W}$ |
| `pos_error_envelope_m` | `double[3]` (m)      | Bounded spatial uncertainty semi-axes $(e_x, e_y, e_z)$                                         | Conservative upper bounds on perception uncertainty; $0 \le e_i \le r_i$              |
| `task_tolerance_m`     | `double[3]` (m)      | Allowable goal region semi-axes $(r_x, r_y, r_z)$                                               | Must meet task profile tolerances; defines $\mathcal{G}_{\text{goal}}$                |
| `max_linear_vel_mps`   | `double` (m/s)       | Requested tool center point speed ceiling $v_{\max}$                                            | Clamped to plant ceiling; verified against dynamic transit time                       |
| `max_wrench`           | `double[6]` (N, N·m) | Maximum effort ceiling $[F_x, F_y, F_z, \tau_x, \tau_y, \tau_z]$                                | Must not exceed structural yield or sensor saturation limits                          |
| `lease_duration_ms`    | `uint32_t` (ms)      | Requested operational validity horizon $\tau_{\text{lease}}$                                    | Clamped to target-evidence horizon $\tau_{\text{ev}}$ and stopping deadline           |
| `fallback_policy_id`   | `uint32_t` (enum)    | Advisory terminal mode (`HOLD`, `STOP`, `TORQUE_OFF`)                                           | Advisory only; Safety MCU overrides based on load and contact state                   |

: **Untrusted intent proposal fields**: Layout and validation invariants of the candidate proposal transmitted from the Application Processor across the proposal boundary. {#tbl-10-intent-proposal-fields tbl-colwidths="[20,17,33,30]"}

None of these outputs, regardless of model size or prompt engineering, constitutes a certified target. SayCan [@ahn2022saycan] multiplies a large language model (LLM)'s semantic prior by a learned value function for each pretrained skill, providing a task ranking conditioned on training data rather than a physical safety veto. VoxPoser [@huang2023voxposer] (@fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka) has an LLM generate Python code that rasterizes 3D attraction and repulsion value maps in voxel space, yet gradient descent over a cost map guarantees neither collision freedom nor joint torque limits. Code as Policies [@liang2023code] writes reactive control scripts that call perception APIs, yet a generated script can enter an infinite loop or stall on edge cases. OK-Robot [@liu2024okrobot] (@fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding) filters candidate grasps using language-conditioned masks, producing a candidate 6-DoF pose without an execution lease or stopping guarantee. @Tbl-10-grounding-paradigms summarizes what each paradigm emits and what the downstream physical permission path must independently verify.

::: {#fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Manipulator 3D affordance grounding via synthesized value maps**: VoxPoser composes language-guided 3D value maps for robotic manipulation tasks [@huang2023voxposer]. An LLM generates code that establishes 3D attraction fields (green) pulling the end effector toward the target and repulsion fields (red) pushing away from obstacles. The resulting spatial cost fields guide trajectory optimization; however, an independent permission path, torque check, and stopping wrapper remain mandatory before motor actuation. (Source: Huang et al., 2023 [@huang2023voxposer], CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="VoxPoser research figure showing a manipulator and sequential language-guided 3D spatial value maps for several tabletop tasks. The image illustrates proposed objectives and motion planning, not a certified force limit, collision bound, or intent lease. Source: Huang et al., 2023."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_grounded_affordance_franka.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

In @fig-10-real-grounded-affordance-franka, Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer] illustrate how an LLM synthesizes spatial cost volumes directly in the robot's physical workspace. Given instructions such as "open the top drawer" or "sort the cans into the basket," the model writes code that populates a 3D voxel grid with numerical potential values. Attraction fields pull the end effector toward affordance targets (such as drawer handles or grasping points), while repulsion fields build potential barriers around visual obstacles. A trajectory optimizer computes paths by descending the negative gradient of the combined field. However, cost fields alone certify neither collision freedom nor actuator feasibility: an unvalidated gradient descent can command joint velocities that exceed inverter limits or drive the tool center point into transparent glass barriers that generated no depth returns.

::: {#fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Open-vocabulary grasp grounding pipeline**: OK-Robot combines candidate grasp generation with language-conditioned object selection and geometric filtering [@liu2024okrobot]. An open-vocabulary detector isolates the target object mask, candidate grasps are sampled across the 3D point cloud, and geometric heuristics prune inadmissible approaches. The resulting grasp pose represents a candidate proposal; bounding tolerances, evidence deadlines, and independent permission checks are an architectural wrapper developed in this chapter. (Source: Liu et al., 2024 [@liu2024okrobot], CC BY 4.0)." fig-alt="OK-Robot figure showing a robot camera view, candidate grasps, a language-conditioned target mask, filtering, and a selected grasp pose. The image illustrates proposal generation; it does not show a certified collision check or an expiring intent lease."}
![](images/jpg/fig10_real_open_vocab_grounding.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

In @fig-10-real-open-vocab-grounding, Liu et al. [-@liu2024okrobot] demonstrate open-vocabulary grasping by decoupling semantic object identification from geometric grasp generation. The robot captures an RGB-D camera view of a cluttered tabletop. An open-vocabulary 2D detector (e.g., OWL-ViT) isolates the segmentation mask corresponding to the target prompt ("blue mug"). Concurrently, an unconditioned 3D grasp sampler (AnyGrasp) evaluates candidate 6-DoF gripper poses across the entire scene point cloud. The pipeline filters these candidates by retaining only grasps whose contact surfaces align with the segmented object mask while passing geometric collision heuristics. However, the selected grasp pose remains an unvalidated geometric hypothesis: it carries no temporal evidence epoch, no physical contact force ceiling, and no expiring intent lease, meaning that a software stall during downstream execution can leave the robot executing a blind approach long after the target object has shifted.

| Proposal source           | Representation sent downstream                          | Early check                                                | Remaining evidence needed                                                                        |
|:--------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 2D box or mask            | Image region plus measured depth and camera calibration | Reject absent depth or a target outside a validated region | 3D pose error, occlusion, object identity, and swept-path clearance                              |
| 3D feature or value field | Candidate target or cost field in a stated frame        | Reject out-of-workspace targets and stale map cells        | Conservative occupancy, unknown-space policy, actuator and timing bounds                         |
| Action-token VLA          | Decoded action in its trained action range              | Reject out-of-range or inadmissible proposals              | State-dependent physical limit and independent permission; token bins provide no clearance proof |
| Language-selected skill   | Skill identifier with estimated success                 | Rank or decline low-confidence candidates                  | Current preconditions, path feasibility, and separate physical enforcement                       |

: **Grounding representations and admission questions**: Outputs from different model families require different conversions before a physical permission check. {#tbl-10-grounding-paradigms tbl-colwidths="[18,24,24,34]"}
Discretized outputs carry no metric bound, and the two common kinds lack it for different reasons.[^fn-vla-action-discretization] In action-token models such as RT-1 [@brohan2023rt1] and OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], a decoded token is an empirical index within a normalized training distribution that encodes zero metric clearance to physical obstacles. In vision-language models such as PaliGemma, location tokens quantize normalized image coordinates, which become a metric base-frame pose only through measured depth, a sensor calibration chain, and an uncertainty model whose extrinsic and depth terms can easily dominate the quantization grid itself.

[^fn-vla-action-discretization]: **Action and Location Token Discretization**\index{Vision-language-action!token discretization}: Vision-language-action architectures discretize continuous joint or Cartesian deltas into uniform bins (typically 256 per dimension) over an empirical training range, discarding continuous metric clearance. Similarly, multimodal backbones with location tokens map normalized image coordinates into discrete spatial bins (for example, 1,024 bins in PaliGemma), requiring external camera intrinsics and optical depth unprojection to recover metric coordinates in the robot's physical workspace.

To prevent a learned output from masquerading as a deterministic setpoint, the producer must retain the referent identity and the dated evidence that selected it. Its observation record may contain bounding boxes, attention weights, class probabilities, and a full oriented covariance estimate. The intent proposal (@sec-intent-lease) links to the belief record built from that observation (@sec-memory-spatial-state-schema) by digest and evidence epoch; it carries a candidate pose, conservative base-frame error bounds, task tolerances, and requested expiry, not those full producer-side fields. The independent permission path checks the linked evidence and request against its own limits. An object can shift or become occluded after camera exposure, so a coordinate without a valid evidence link and deadline cannot remain an authorized target.

When a vision-language model sees multiple candidate objects, an argmax can hide an unresolved choice. A digital recommendation can still mislead a user, but it has no direct actuator path; in a robot, an admitted spatial proposal can move mass. If a red glass jar sits beside the red mug on the takeaway conveyor, a poorly grounded guess may select the jar. The system should preserve candidate identity and calibrated uncertainty, refusing a proposal when a task-specific ambiguity threshold is exceeded. The permission path then maintains a feasible hold or stop while the producer seeks a clearer observation or instruction.

Formally, **open-vocabulary grounding ambiguity**\index{Grounding!ambiguity} is the condition where multimodal feature projections yield multi-peak posterior distributions, overlapping geometric hypotheses, or unresolvable evidential ties across candidate physical referents, requiring an explicit grounding refusal (`ERR_GROUNDING_AMBIGUITY`) rather than optimistic argmax tie-breaking. A high entropy over the candidate-referent distribution $\mathbf{z}$, $H(\mathbf{z}) > H_{\text{thresh}}$, is one signal of it, and the producer-side filter of @fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease can refuse on that signal before the proposal crosses the proposal boundary. The test that must hold for every proposal is an independent count of the candidates in the pick window (@sec-intent-failure-modes), because a confidently wrong model can report low entropy.

::: {#fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Grounded intent pipeline architecture across the silicon boundary**: Physical AI system architecture partitioning high-capacity deliberative reasoning on the Application Processor (AP) from deterministic safety enforcement on the real-time Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU). The AP processes multimodal streams (RGB-D vision, natural language prompts, proprioception) through a vision-language backbone and 3D spatial field generator. A producer-side entropy filter ($H(\\mathbf{z}) \\le H_{\\text{thresh}}$) rejects ambiguous bimodal hypotheses before passing a structured intent proposal across the inter-core shared memory boundary (e.g., RPMSG over SRAM). The MCU independently verifies evidence epochs, physical actuator ceilings, and braking stopping reserve before arming a hardware countdown timer and admitting motion (synthesized from Huang et al. [-@huang2023voxposer], Ahn et al. [-@ahn2022saycan], and Gray [-@gray1989leases])." fig-alt="Diagram of vision, prompt, and robot state entering a vision-language backbone and candidate 3D cost field on the Application Processor. A producer-side entropy filter can reject the proposal. A bounded record crosses a silicon boundary via RPMSG/SRAM to a Safety MCU, which checks evidence, physical limits, and stopping feasibility before granting actuator permission."}
![](images/svg/fig10_vla_cross_attention_intent_lease.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-10-vla-cross-attention-intent-lease, the architecture enforces physical safety by physically separating the compute environments across a silicon boundary:

- *Application Processor (AP Domain):* Running a non-real-time operating system (such as Linux) on multi-core host CPUs and neural accelerators, the AP processes computationally intensive visual and linguistic models. Multimodal inputs (RGB-D video, joint telemetry, natural language task instructions) enter a cross-attention vision-language backbone. If candidate referent features indicate high entropy ($H(\mathbf{z}) > H_{\text{thresh}}$), a producer-side filter immediately flags semantic ambiguity. Otherwise, the AP packages the candidate goal, requested wrench limits, and parent belief digest into a static intent proposal message.
- *Inter-Core Transport Boundary:* The proposal crosses from the AP to the real-time core via a deterministic, bounded communication channel, such as the Remote Processor Messaging (RPMSG) protocol operating over dedicated shared SRAM rings.
- *Safety Microcontroller Unit (MCU Domain):* Executing a hard real-time operating system (RTOS) or bare-metal control loop, the Safety MCU acts as an untrusted gatekeeper. It treats the incoming proposal purely as an unverified candidate. The MCU validates the evidence epoch against its local monotonic hardware clock, evaluates static workspace and dynamic reachability bounds, checks requested force and velocity limits against configured plant ceilings, and verifies that a collision-free emergency stop profile remains executable within current clearance. Only when all physical invariants are satisfied does the MCU arm a hardware countdown timer ($\tau_{\text{lease}}$) and grant transient tracking authority.

```{python}
#| label: calc-intent-handle-ellipsoid
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
# │ The mug-handle localization estimate as a 95 percent region, compared with  │
# │ the mug's grasp tolerance axis by axis.                                     │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
import math

# ┌── 1. LOAD: illustrative single-view localization model ────────────────────
sigma_lat_x = 4.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (distant pre-approach wrist-camera view, lateral std. dev.)
sigma_lat_y = 5.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera lateral std. dev.)
sigma_depth = 12.0 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (wrist-camera depth std. dev.)
chi2_3dof_95 = 7.815  # category: constant (chi-square quantile, 3 degrees of freedom, 0.95)

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE: principal semi-axes of the 95 percent region ────────────────
k_region = math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95)
semi_x = (k_region * sigma_lat_x).to(millimeter)
semi_y = (k_region * sigma_lat_y).to(millimeter)
semi_z = (k_region * sigma_depth).to(millimeter)
chi2_cdf = math.erf(math.sqrt(chi2_3dof_95 / 2)) - math.sqrt(2 * chi2_3dof_95 / math.pi) * math.exp(-chi2_3dof_95 / 2)

# ┌── 3. GUARD: the claims the prose makes ────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(chi2_cdf - 0.95) < 1e-4, "7.815 is the 0.95 chi-square quantile for 3 degrees of freedom")
check(semi_x < AISLE.grasp_tolerance and semi_y < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Lateral semi-axes fit the grasp tolerance")
check(semi_z > AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Depth semi-axis exceeds the grasp tolerance")
check(AISLE.grasp_initial_error < AISLE.grasp_tolerance, "Admitted handle estimate fits the tolerance")

# ┌── 4. OUTPUT: rendered values ──────────────────────────────────────────────
class HandleEllipsoid:
    sigma_x_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_x, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_y_str = fmt_length(sigma_lat_y, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    sigma_z_str = fmt_length(sigma_depth, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    chi2_str = fmt(chi2_3dof_95, precision=3, commas=False)
    semi_x_str = fmt_length(semi_x, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_y_str = fmt_length(semi_y, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    semi_z_str = fmt_length(semi_z, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider the grounding model's estimate of the red mug's handle from a single wrist-camera view taken at a distance, before the arm begins its approach. In an illustrative calibrated Gaussian localization model, the principal sensor-frame standard deviations are `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_x_str`, `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_y_str`, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.sigma_z_str`, the largest along the camera's depth axis, which is also the gripper's approach axis. A **95 percent statistical region** around the estimated handle position $\mathbf{p}_0$ uses Mahalanobis squared distance $(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0)^T\mathbf{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{p}-\mathbf{p}_0)\le\chi^2_{3,0.95}$, where the three-degree-of-freedom quantile is `{python} HandleEllipsoid.chi2_str`, yielding principal semi-axes `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_x_str`, `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_y_str`, and `{python} HandleEllipsoid.semi_z_str`. @Fig-10-intent-lease-envelope contrasts that uncertain target with the mug's `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.r_tol_str` grasp tolerance. Both lateral semi-axes fit inside the tolerance, but the depth semi-axis does not, so this estimate fails admission and needs better sensing, a different approach, or refusal.

The pick admitted in @sec-intent-lease rests on better sensing. Its belief record (@sec-memory-spatial-state-schema) comes from a closer wrist-camera capture on the approach, which bounds the initial error at `{python} IntentLeaseArchetypes.e0_str`. Even that admitted estimate's 95 percent region leaves a residual tail and cannot by itself certify clearance, so the intent proposal carries conservative base-frame error bounds rather than claiming to encode this covariance.

::: {#fig-10-intent-lease-envelope fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Localization uncertainty and authority expiry**: Panel (a) sketches a statistical target-uncertainty ellipsoid beside the grasp's separate task tolerance. Panel (b) compares counterfactual traces: blue expires and brakes, green continues only with fresh renewals, and red shows motion without a lease. Whether the blue trace rests before the obstacle depends on total pre-brake delay, deceleration, and clearance." fig-alt="Panel (a) shows target-position uncertainty beside the grasp's separate task tolerance region. Panel (b) compares alternative velocity traces: blue authority expires then braking reaches rest if feasible; green dots show fresh renewals in a separate scenario; red continues without a lease toward the obstacle. Physical clearance depends on the complete stopping budget."}
![](images/svg/fig10_intent_lease_envelope.svg){width="100%"}
:::

In @fig-10-intent-lease-envelope, the two panels illustrate the dual constraints of spatial localization uncertainty and temporal lease enforcement:

- *Panel (a): Spatial Uncertainty Ellipsoid vs. Task Tolerance:* The blue wireframe ellipsoid depicts the 95 percent confidence region of the mug-handle localization estimate $\mathbf{p}_0$ under the calibrated Gaussian covariance $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. Because optical triangulation uncertainty along the camera optical axis scales quadratically with distance ($z$) and inversely with stereo baseline ($B$), the standard deviation along depth ($\sigma_z = 12\text{ mm}$) is roughly three times larger than lateral standard deviations ($\sigma_x = 4\text{ mm}, \sigma_y = 5\text{ mm}$). Scaling by the 3-DoF chi-square factor $k = \sqrt{\chi^2_{3,0.95}} \approx 2.80$ produces principal semi-axes of $11.2\text{ mm}$ ($x$), $14.0\text{ mm}$ ($y$), and $33.5\text{ mm}$ ($z$). The dashed circle represents the physical task clearance boundary $r_{\text{tol}} = 15\text{ mm}$. While lateral uncertainty fits inside this tolerance, the elongated depth semi-axis ($33.5\text{ mm}$) pierces the boundary by more than a factor of two. Admitting this uncertain goal directly would risk gripper collision or finger stubbing; the system must either capture closer observations or reject the proposal.
- *Panel (b): Counterfactual Execution Traces:* This panel plots robot velocity over time across three distinct architectural paradigms:
  1. *Unleased Open-Loop Execution (Solid Red Curve):* The system commands motion toward the target at constant cruise velocity. When an unexpected obstacle blocks the path or upstream computation hangs, the robot lacks an expiring lease. It continues driving open-loop until crashing violently into the obstacle at full speed.
  2. *Continuous Active Renewal (Dashed Green Curve):* As the robot moves, high-rate local perception ($50\text{ Hz}$) continuously re-estimates target coordinates, issuing fresh leases before the current lease expires ($T_{\text{renew}} < \tau_{\text{lease}}$). This enables seamless, continuous tracking toward dynamic targets.
  3. *Expiring Lease with Assured Fallback (Solid Blue Curve):* An intent lease is granted with hardware deadline $t_{\text{exp}}$. When an upstream stall occurs and no renewal packet arrives, the Safety MCU automatically revokes motion authority at $t_{\text{exp}}$. Rather than freezing open-loop, the controller engages a pre-validated braking profile that safely dissipates kinetic energy to bring the robot to rest before violating physical obstacle clearance.

A detection with a large uncertainty estimate can be rejected by a configured statistical gate. A confident grounding to the wrong physical entity can pass that gate. Suppose instead that a thin-walled glass jar arrives alone where the mug should be, and the vision-language model assigns it a high confidence score when asked for the red mug. The model emits a sharp, low-variance geometric proposal centered on the glass. The trajectory planner receives the coordinate, computes an $SE(3)$ inverse kinematics solution, verifies joint limits, and confirms that the path clears all obstacles in the static environment map. The permission path may find the proposed motion within its configured geometric and force bounds. If those bounds allow the grip force the ceramic mug needs, a smooth, geometrically valid trajectory can crush the glass despite passing the checks.

This failure reveals the boundary between what the permission path can verify and what it must accept as an unvalidated premise. The permission path checks coordinate bounds, kinematic reachability, joint torque limits, and geometric collisions against known occupancy grids. Those physical checks do not establish that the coordinate names the intended object, so the premise that the grasped object is the named object lies outside the permission path's reach. It needs its own task evidence, and it travels with the mug into the handover branch of the release case (@sec-release-case-worked-full) and into the register of claims the machine's evidence leaves open (@sec-frontier-residual-claims-register).

Multimodal feature extraction, cross-attention alignment, and open-vocabulary phrase grounding belong to the computer vision and language literature [@kamath2021mdetr; @gu2022open; @radford2021learning; @liu2023grounding]. A physical AI architecture consumes these grounding models without relying on their internal activations for safety, and even a filtered proposal stream still needs the independent motion-permission check. AutoRT's language-model task filter raised the fraction of acceptable proposed tasks yet still passed a small fraction of unsafe ones, and its deployment relied on joint-force pausing, emergency stops, and human supervision rather than on the prompt (\ref{ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution}) [@ahn2023autort].

::: {#ws-intent-autort-hallucination-constitution .callout-war-story title="AutoRT task filtering and supervision (2024)"}
**Context**: AutoRT deployed foundation models to propose and filter physical manipulation tasks for fleets of mobile manipulators operating in unstructured human office environments [@ahn2023autort].

**Mechanism**: In an empirical sample of 259 proposed tasks, 228 were initially judged acceptable by human annotators. Applying a secondary large language model as a "constitutional" affordance and safety filter improved retention (200 of 214 retained tasks were acceptable), raising the acceptable fraction from 88 to 93 percent. However, the semantic filter still permitted 14 unsuitable or unsafe tasks to pass through to execution.

**Impact**: Relying strictly on high-level prompting or semantic filtering left open a non-negligible tail of hazardous proposals, demonstrating that ungrounded foundation models cannot self-certify physical safety or guarantee collision-free execution in open environments.

**Response**: The system architecture placed physical safety outside the model's domain: deployments supplemented learned proposals with hardware joint-force limits, physical emergency stop buttons, and direct human line-of-sight supervision or physical perimeter barricades.

**Systems lesson**: A learned task filter can improve proposal quality, but it cannot serve as a safety referee. An independent, deterministic permission and fallback path must validate every physical action against real-time plant limits before execution.
:::

Whatever its source, a grounded target is also a claim about a moment. The red mug that the model selected correctly at capture keeps moving with the conveyor, so a proposal that was right when issued becomes wrong with no change to its contents. It must therefore carry a deadline that the permission path can enforce without the model.

## Expiring Goals and Temporal Validity Leases {#sec-intent-goals-expire}

In physical AI, where computational commands drive real-world actuators across continuous physical state spaces, granting open-ended motion authority is hazardous. A high-level goal proposed by a neural intent model—such as reaching for a moving workpiece or navigating through an aisle—is valid only within a specific temporal window governed by physical target motion and sensor degradation. When an autonomous machine executes a goal, continuous physical states (moving mass, closing clearance, drifting obstacles) evolve independently of computational inference. If the computational engine executing the model stalls, delays, or crashes, the machine must never continue blindly tracking a stale objective. Physical AI architectures enforce motion safety through temporal validity leases: time-bounded execution contracts that automatically expire on monotonic hardware clocks unless affirmatively renewed with fresh physical evidence.

To see why goal expiration must be autonomous and time-bounded, suppose the application processor hangs while the arm reaches for the red mug. The fault that makes cancellation necessary is the same fault that stops the cancellation from being sent, because an explicit abort requires a working sender, scheduler, and communication path. An intent lease must therefore expire on its own. This is principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission} applied to a goal. In distributed systems, Gray and Cheriton [-@gray1989leases] introduced leases to ensure cache consistency without distributed commit protocols: a coordinator grants time-bounded authority that lapses automatically unless renewed, eliminating blocking when a client crashes. In physical AI, the authority relationship is reversed: the privileged Safety MCU acts as the real-time resource coordinator, granting a transient tracking lease to the unprivileged deliberative layer. If the host operating system stalls, deadlocks in a garbage-collection pause, or crashes under a kernel panic, the Safety MCU does not negotiate or wait for an abort packet: its local hardware countdown timer lapses, atomically revoking tracking authority and engaging an independent, pre-certified fallback profile.[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Kinetic momentum budgets and stopping distance constraints originate in @sec-body-kinetic-momentum.
:::

Crucially, the lease duration is never evaluated against general-purpose system wall-clock time (such as POSIX `CLOCK_REALTIME`), which can jump unpredictably due to Network Time Protocol (NTP) adjustments or leap seconds. Instead, intent leases are clocked strictly by monotonic hardware timer registers on the Safety MCU silicon, driven by dedicated crystal oscillators that advance uniformly regardless of software state.

The target-evidence deadline follows the rate at which the physical target can diverge from its last measurement. Suppose validated bounds cap relative target drift at $v_{\text{drift}}$ (representing the maximum relative velocity divergence between the robot end-effector frame and the physical target, incorporating both workpiece conveyor motion and unmodeled robot base odometry drift) and initial position error at $e_0$ within the belief record's declared validity region, and the task allows a target error of $r_{\text{tol}}$. Over elapsed time $\Delta t$, unobserved physical divergence expands linearly: $\|\mathbf{x}^*(t) - \hat{\mathbf{x}}(t_0)\| \le e_0 + v_{\text{drift}} \Delta t$. Setting this maximum error equal to the task tolerance boundary $r_{\text{tol}}$ yields the **target-evidence horizon**:
$$\tau_{\text{ev}} \le \frac{r_{\text{tol}} - e_0}{v_{\text{drift}}}$$ {#eq-intent-lease-drift-bound}

[^fn-hw-watchdog-rtt]: **Hardware watchdog down-counters**\index{Hardware!watchdog timer}: Detecting a missed renewal is only the first term of the response budget. Drive command propagation, brake engagement, and physical deceleration each add a separately measured term.

When $r_{\text{tol}}\le e_0$, the target is inadmissible at capture: sensor uncertainty alone exceeds the task clearance, and the controller immediately refuses dependent motion.
